notes: Section 68 cargo-fire arbitration challenge; Sir Anthony Evans dismissed on s73, time and abuse grounds.

enrichment.short_title: Thyssen Canada v Mariana Maritime: section 68 challenge to cargo fire award dismissed
key_facts: Cargo owners challenged an arbitration award finding no unseaworthiness after a fire in Hold 3 of the vessel Mariana on 9 June 1998.
The tribunal had accepted that a smouldering cigarette left during loading at Constanza caused the fire and that owners exercised due diligence.
After the hearing the claimants obtained post-award evidence from crew alleging hot work and a conspiracy to conceal the true cause.
The section 68 application was made about five months late and the claimants had known of Mr Katsarakis's hot-work account before the award was published.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court application under section 68(2)(g) of the Arbitration Act 1996 to set aside or remit a cargo-damage arbitration award, with an extension of time under section 80(5).
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no extension of time granted and no adjournment for trial of perjury/fraud.
enrichment.ratio: A section 68(2)(g) challenge requires proof of fraud or procuration contrary to public policy; a party who continues in the arbitration with knowledge of the alleged irregularity, or could with reasonable diligence have discovered it, loses the right to object under section 73 and cannot obtain an extension of time.
legal_issues: Whether the claimants lost the right to object under section 73 by continuing in the arbitration after learning of alleged perjured evidence
Whether an extension of time should be granted for a late section 68 application
Whether fresh post-award evidence of hot work justified setting aside the award for fraud or public policy
Whether the application was an abuse of process
linked_authorities: Profilati v Paine Webber [2001] 1 Lloyd's Rep 715
Rustal v Gill & Duffus SA [2000] 1 Lloyd's Rep 14
Kalmneft v Glencore International AG [2002] 1 Lloyd's Rep 128

confidence.notes: Statutory analysis and dismissal on multiple independent grounds are clearly reasoned.

notes: Complex immigration/RRA tangle; Hughes J held s104(4) abandonment did not bar County Court discrimination claim.

enrichment.short_title: Bibi v IAT: immigration appeal abandonment and Race Relations Act jurisdiction
key_facts: A Bangladeshi applicant appealed refusal of entry clearance for herself and two children, alleging both lack of genuine visitor intention and unlawful discrimination by the entry clearance officer.
The adjudicator allowed the appeal on the merits but failed to determine the discrimination ground contrary to section 86(2).
After visas were granted the Immigration Appeal Tribunal treated the appeal as abandoned under section 104(4).
The claimant sought judicial review to preserve determination of her Race Relations Act complaint.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of an Immigration Appeal Tribunal notice treating an immigration appeal as abandoned after grant of leave to enter.
enrichment.outcome: Application for judicial review dismissed; the Tribunal was correct to treat the appeal as abandoned, but the claimant retained a route to pursue discrimination in the County Court.
enrichment.ratio: Section 57A(1) temporarily ousts County Court jurisdiction only while an immigration appeal is pending or could be brought; once the appeal ends by abandonment under section 104(4), a discrimination claim may be brought within six months under section 68(2A), even if the immigration merits succeeded.
legal_issues: Whether section 104(4) prevented adjudication of an undecided discrimination ground of appeal
Whether the adjudicator erred in failing to determine the section 84(1)(b) discrimination ground
Construction of section 57A and its interaction with section 68(2A)
Whether a discrimination complaint survives as a separate component of a composite appeal
index_terms: E v Entry Clearance Officer for Lagos
linked_authorities: E v Entry Clearance Officer for Lagos [2004] UKIAT (IAT decision of 14 December 2004)

confidence.notes: Statutory scheme and outcome are clearly explained, though some procedural routes were expressly left open.

notes: Planning s288 challenge; Collins J quashed inspector's refusal of health club change of use.

enrichment.short_title: Hammersmatch v FSS: health club change of use appeal quashed
key_facts: The claimant sought planning permission to change part of a largely empty industrial building in Welwyn Garden City from B1 employment use to a health and fitness club.
An inspector dismissed a section 78 appeal against non-determination, refusing permission on employment-land and sequential leisure policy grounds.
The building had stood largely empty for about five years and the scheme was said to be the only feasible way to regenerate it.
Collins J found the inspector's sequential test and employment-land conclusions flawed and unsupported by the evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to an inspector's decision dismissing an appeal under section 78 and refusing planning permission.
enrichment.outcome: Inspector's decision quashed and the case remitted for reconsideration.
enrichment.ratio: Where need for leisure facilities was accepted but identified alternative sites were speculative, distant or policy-inconsistent, it was unreasonable to reject an accessible out-of-centre site; limiting regeneration to local plan processes also misapplied employment-area policy.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector properly applied Policy CLT2 and the PPG6 sequential approach to leisure development
Whether the proposed use was an appropriate use of employment land under Policy EMP2
Whether the inspector's findings on need and alternative sites were supported by evidence
Whether failure to refer expressly to section 54A indicated error

confidence.notes: Both main issues were found unsustainable and quashing was clearly ordered.

notes: Asylum appeal remitted; IAT failed to identify material error of law per CA v SSHD.

enrichment.short_title: Pajaziti v SSHD: asylum appeal remitted for inadequate IAT reasons
key_facts: An ethnic Albanian from the Presevo Valley claimed asylum after fleeing police action linked to his father's LDK/KLA activity.
The adjudicator found a well-founded fear of persecution and breach of Article 3, relying partly on expert evidence conflicting with country material.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal allowed the Secretary of State's appeal but failed distinctly to identify an error of law by the adjudicator.
The Secretary of State conceded that the IAT had not approached its jurisdiction correctly following CA v SSHD.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision allowing the Secretary of State's appeal against an adjudicator's asylum and Article 3 determination.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; matter remitted to a differently constituted Immigration Appeal Tribunal.
enrichment.ratio: An appeal cannot be allowed unless the Tribunal distinctly holds that the adjudicator made a material error of law; where the adjudicator preferred one expert report over country information and prior tribunal decisions without adequate analysis, arguable errors of law warrant remittal rather than upholding the adjudicator.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT identified a material error of law as required by CA v SSHD
Whether the adjudicator adequately analysed conflicting country and expert evidence on conditions in the Presevo Valley
Whether the adjudicator properly addressed prior tribunal decisions requiring exceptional circumstances
Whether the court should uphold the adjudicator or remit the Secretary of State's appeal
linked_authorities: CA v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] EWCA Civ 1165
Mlauzi v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2005] EWCA Civ 128
Zejnullahu v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2002] UKIAT 05130

confidence.notes: Concession, remittal order and arguable-error analysis are explicit.

notes: Interlocutory refusal to adjourn quarry appeal; Chadwick LJ prioritised legal certainty.

enrichment.short_title: Stancliffe Stone v Peak District: adjournment of quarry appeal refused
key_facts: Stancliffe Stone sought declarations that 1952 planning permission still permitted reopening dormant quarries at Stanton Moor in the Peak District.
Moore-Bick J dismissed the claim, holding the permission spent or inapplicable to Endcliffe and Lees Cross quarries.

The authority and quarry operator jointly sought to adjourn the listed appeal for at least two years while negotiating a section 106 deal to trade Dale View extension for abandonment of the dormant sites.
The parish council opposed prolonging legal uncertainty.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to adjourn a pending Court of Appeal hearing in Part 8 proceedings concerning the status of historic mineral planning permission.
enrichment.outcome: Adjournment application dismissed; appeal remained listed for hearing.
enrichment.ratio: It is not the function of the Court of Appeal to prolong legal uncertainty to assist negotiations between a planning authority and developer where proceedings were originally brought for urgent certainty.
legal_issues: Whether adjournment was in the public interest pending possible section 106 negotiations
Whether legal uncertainty assisted or hindered proper planning outcomes
Whether active or dormant quarry status under Schedule 13 turned on one or several 1952 consents

confidence.notes: Interlocutory disposition and reasoning are clear though merits of the underlying appeal were not decided.

notes: Long TCC judgment on Great Eastern Hotel delay; Laing liable for critical delay and substantial damages items.

enrichment.short_title: Great Eastern Hotel v Laing: construction manager delay damages
key_facts: Great Eastern Hotel claimed damages from John Laing as construction manager for about 44 weeks' delay in refurbishing and extending the Great Eastern Hotel.
GEH alleged lost revenue and substantial additional professional and trade contractor costs exceeding £17 million.
HHJ Bowsher found Laing breached the construction management agreement and was wholly responsible for critical delay in key periods.
Damages were assessed item by item, with partial recovery on lost profits, professional fees and miscellaneous delay costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial of a damages claim and counterclaim arising from a construction management agreement dated 30 April 1998.
enrichment.outcome: Laing held liable for culpable delay; GEH recovered substantial but not full claimed losses, with final money judgment form to be settled after further submissions.
enrichment.ratio: A construction manager who breaches programme management obligations and causes critical delay is liable for foreseeable consequential losses, but claimants must prove causation and quantum rigorously, including discounting alleged revenue ramp-up not supported by comparable occupancy evidence.
legal_issues: Whether Laing breached the construction management agreement and caused critical delay
Assessment of lost profit during the delay period including ramp-up methodology
Recoverability of additional professional team fees caused by prolongation
Quantum of miscellaneous relocation, security and storage costs

confidence.notes: Very long judgment with detailed liability and quantum findings; final monetary order was left to further argument.

notes: Landmark Re U judgment refusing Taylor v Lawrence reopening of factitious injury finding.

enrichment.short_title: Re U: Taylor v Lawrence application to reopen child care appeal refused
key_facts: Bracewell J found that mother U had deliberately suffocated her daughter on multiple occasions; permission to appeal was refused and Kirkwood J later ordered adoption.
The mother applied under CPR 52.17/Taylor v Lawrence to reopen the refusal of permission, relying on fresh medical evidence including Professor D's GOR theory.
The parents were found to have deceived professionals and the court, undermining late histories given to new experts.
The court refused the application and criticised case management and attacks on the guardian's impartiality.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application under CPR 52.17 to reopen a finally determined refusal of permission to appeal in care proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; no permission to reopen; costs ordered against the applicant.
enrichment.ratio: The Taylor v Lawrence jurisdiction requires exceptional circumstances and real injustice from a corrupted process, not merely fresh evidence that might have affected the outcome; Ladd v Marshall principles do not suffice for a second appeal, and late expert evidence based on discredited parental accounts cannot meet that threshold.
legal_issues: Scope of CPR 52.17 and Taylor v Lawrence to reopen a final permission decision
Distinction between fresh evidence on first appeal and reopening on Ladd v Marshall grounds
Whether new medical evidence on gastro-oesophageal reflux undermined findings of deliberate suffocation
Role and independence of the children's guardian in expert meetings

confidence.notes: Detailed treatment of Taylor v Lawrence and explicit refusal with comprehensive reasoning.

notes: Trap Grounds village green guidance; Carnwath LJ answered registration issues of principle.

enrichment.short_title: Oxfordshire v Oxford City: Trap Grounds village green registration guidance
key_facts: Users sought registration of the Trap Grounds in North Oxford as a town or village green to resist housing development by Oxford City Council.
The land was scrubland and reed beds formerly owned by St John's College and used informally for dog-walking and recreation.
Lightman J had made detailed declarations on registration issues; the appeal concerned the amended class (c) definition after 30 January 2001.
Carnwath LJ gave guidance on ten issues of law, leaving some factual evaluation questions to the registration authority.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal guidance on preliminary issues in an appeal concerning registration of land as a town or village green under the amended Commons Registration Act definition.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; detailed declarations replaced by guidance that the authority must decide the application according to stated principles.
enrichment.ratio: Registration as a class (c) green is conclusive that land is a town or village green for the historic statutory protection regime but does not itself confer public sports and pastimes rights; under the amended definition lawful use must continue to the date of registration, and authorities may treat or amend applications to refer to lesser areas.
legal_issues: Effect of registration as a class (c) green on public rights
Meaning of 'continue to do so' in the amended village green definition
Whether applications after 30 January 2001 engage only the amended definition
Whether part of the Trap Grounds could be registered and whether user issues were for the authority

confidence.notes: Ten numbered rulings are clearly set out, though issues (ix) and (x) were reserved as factual.

notes: Workplace harassment appeal dismissed; statutory tort and primary duty claims failed on facts.

enrichment.short_title: Banks v Ablex: workplace harassment and stress claim dismissed
key_facts: A night shift supervisor at a CD factory claimed psychiatric injury caused by aggressive conduct of engineer Chris Briggs from early 1998 to October 1998.
The county court rejected an assault allegation and later claims for intentional infliction of harm, harassment and employer negligence.
Briggs was volatile and had received a formal warning in March 1998, but the claimant was regarded as tough and gave as good as she got.
The Court of Appeal upheld findings that there was no course of conduct harassing the claimant and no foreseeable psychiatric injury.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claimant's appeal from a two-stage county court trial determining preliminary facts then dismissing harassment, negligence and constructive dismissal claims.
enrichment.ratio: Harassment under the 1997 Act requires a course of conduct on at least two occasions directed at the same victim; isolated workplace rudeness by a volatile employee, without targeting or foreseeability of psychiatric harm to a resilient supervisor, does not establish the statutory tort or employer liability under Waters v Metropolitan Police Commissioner.
legal_issues: Whether Briggs's conduct amounted to a course of conduct for the purposes of section 1 of the 1997 Act
Whether employers should have foreseen psychiatric injury to the claimant
Whether vicarious liability arose if harassment were proved
Whether the trial judge's fact findings were inadequate
linked_authorities: Waters v Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis [2000] IRLR 720
Thomas v News Group Newspapers Ltd [2002] EMLR 78

confidence.notes: Legal analysis of the 1997 Act and factual review are thorough and the dismissal is clear.

notes: What's on TV cover reproduction; Hart J granted summary judgment on copyright and undertakings.

enrichment.short_title: IPC Media v News Group: comparative advertising and magazine cover copyright
key_facts: IPC published What's on TV and sued News Group for reproducing its magazine front covers in Sun advertisements promoting free TV Mag.
Similar use in 1998 had been settled by contractual undertakings not to copy covers or logos.
News Group relied on fair dealing for criticism/review or reporting current events under section 30.
Mr Justice Hart held the use was comparative advertising that unfairly exploited the claimant's artistic identity and breached the undertakings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery Division summary judgment application for copyright infringement and breach of contractual undertakings.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment for the claimant on copyright and contractual claims; enquiry as to damages ordered; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Copying a magazine cover to identify a comparator product in promotional advertising is not fair dealing under section 30 where the cover's essential function is brand identification for the copyright owner and the defendant uses that identity to advance competing commercial purposes at the owner's expense.
legal_issues: Whether reproduction of front covers was fair dealing for criticism, review or reporting current events
Whether comparative advertising justified use of copyright material without permission
Construction of 1999 undertakings prohibiting copying of any What's on TV cover
Whether the Comparative Advertising Directive assisted the defendant
linked_authorities: ProSieben Media AG v Carlton UK Television Ltd [1999] FSR 610
Ashdown v Telegraph Group Ltd [2002] RPC 235
IPC Magazines Ltd v MGN Ltd [1998] FSR 431

confidence.notes: Summary judgment reasoning on fair dealing and undertakings is explicit and detailed.
